metadata.description:
Case name: Engine Mfrs. Assn. v. South Coast Air Quality Management Dist.

Opinion filed: 2004-04-28

Docket No.: 02-1343

Citations:
• 158 L. Ed. 2d 529
• 124 S. Ct. 1756
• 541 U.S. 246
• 2004 U.S. LEXIS 3232

Case holding summaries:
• “[A] standard is a standard even when not enforced through manufacturer-directed regulation . . . .”
• using dictionary definition to construe Congress' intent in using the word "standard"
• “Statutory construction must begin with the language employed by Congress and the assumption that the ordinary meaning of that language accurately expresses the legislative purpose.”
• “Statutory construction must begin with the language employed by Congress and the assumption that the ordinary meaning of that language accurately expresses the legislative purpose.” (citation omitted)
• "Statutory construction must begin with the language employed by Congress and the assumption that the ordinary meaning of that language accurately expresses the legislative purpose."
• “Statutory construction must begin with the language employed by Congress and the assumption that the ordinary meaning of that language accurately expresses the legislative purpose” (internal quotation marks omitted)
• "Statutory construction must begin with the language employed by Congress and the assumption that the ordinary meaning of that language accurately expresses the legislative purpose" (internal quotation marks omitted)
• “Statutory construction must begin with the language employed by Congress and the assumption that the ordinary meaning of that language accurately expresses the legislative purpose.” (quotation marks omitted)
• "[I]t appears likely that at least certain aspects of the [state law rules] are pre-empted[,] . . . [but] does not necessarily follow . . . that [they] are pre-empted in toto."
• finding preemption under the Clean Air Act although the re- quirements directly targeted car buyers rather than sellers
• stating that it “would make no sense” to allow state regulations to escape preemption because they ad- dressed the purchase, rather than manufacture, of a fed- erally regulated product
• “[A] standard is a standard even when not enforced through manufacturer-directed regulation . . . .”
• “Statutory construction must begin with the language employed by Congress and the assumption that the ordinary meaning of that language accurately expresses the legislative purpose.”
• "Legislation designed to free from pollution the very air that people breathe clearly falls within the exercise of even the most traditional concept of what is compendiously known as the police power"
• applying presumption against preemption to a local regulation
• “Statutory construction must begin with the language employed by Congress and the assumption that the ordinary meaning of that language accurately expresses the legislative purpose.” (internal quotation marks omitted)
• “Statutory construction must begin with the language employed by Congress and the assumption that the ordinary meaning of that language accurately expresses the legislative purpose.” (internal quotation marks omitted)
• adding that “[t]his interpretation is consistent with the use of ‘standard’ throughout Title II of the [Clean Air Act] (which governs emissions from moving sources
